note_claims.claim: The patient is reviewing his diabetes following a hypoglycaemic episode.
The patient experienced a hypoglycaemic episode last Tuesday after skipping lunch while gardening.
The patient's daughter (who has type 1 diabetes) found him confused during the episode.
The patient's daughter measured capillary glucose at 2.8 mmol/L during the episode.
The patient recovered from the episode within 15 minutes.
The patient experiences occasional pre-meal wobbliness.
The patient reports pins and needles in his hands at night, suspected to be carpal tunnel.
The patient has no visual problems, but retinal screening is due.
The patient is prescribed Metformin 1g twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Gliclazide 80 mg twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Atorvastatin 20 mg.
The patient is prescribed Ramipril 5 mg.
The patient's pedal pulses are palpable.
Monofilament sensation is normal in both feet.
The patient has a callus under the ball of the left first metatarsal head.
The patient's blood pressure is 138/84.
The patient's weight is 91 kilos.
The patient's HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol, which is an increase from the previous 58.
The patient's eGFR is 52, which is stable.
The patient has Type 2 diabetes with recent hypoglycaemia on gliclazide.
The patient has stable CKD stage 3a.
The plan is to reduce gliclazide to 80 mg in the morning only.
The plan is to start empagliflozin 10 mg once daily.
The plan includes providing sick day rules and a leaflet regarding empagliflozin.
The plan includes a referral to a podiatrist for the callus.
The plan includes booking a retinal screening.
The plan is to review the patient in three months with repeat HbA1c and kidney tests.
Safety netting includes stopping empagliflozin if the patient experiences vomiting, diarrhoea, or is unable to eat and drink.

transcript_facts.fact: Patient experienced a funny turn involving sweating, shakiness, and inability to think straight.
The hypoglycaemic episode occurred on Tuesday because it was bin day and the patient had skipped lunch.
The relative found the patient confused and identified it as a hypoglycaemia because she has type 1 diabetes.
The relative gave the patient orange juice and biscuits.
The patient recovered within about fifteen minutes.
The relative used a meter and measured the capillary glucose at 2.8.
The patient sometimes feels a bit wobbly before tea.
The patient drives to the shops and to his allotment.
The patient is on Metformin 1 gram twice a day.
The patient is on Gliclazide 80 milligrams twice a day, taken in the morning and at teatime.
The patient is on Atorvastatin 20 milligrams and Ramipril 5 milligrams.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
The patient's feet have been fine.
The relative has pins and needles in her hands at night, which the clinician suspects is carpal tunnel.
The patient has had his eye screening letter.
The patient's HbA1c is 62, which is up from 58 last time.
The patient's kidney function, eGFR, is 52, which is about the same as before.
The clinician noted that sugar control has drifted up a little, but the hypoglycaemia worries him more.
The clinician noted there is a bit of hard skin and a callus under the ball of the left foot, by the big toe.
The patient's blood pressure is 138 over 84.
The patient's weight is 91 kilos.
The clinician suggested reducing the gliclazide dose to 80 milligrams in the morning only and stopping the teatime dose.
The clinician suggested adding empagliflozin 10 milligrams once a day.
The clinician explained sick day rules and gave a leaflet on these rules.
The patient acknowledged the instructions.
The clinician advised the patient to check his blood sugar before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
The clinician advised the patient not to drive if his blood sugar is below five.
The clinician advised the patient to always keep some sugary snacks in the car.
The relative offered to get the patient some glucose tablets.
The clinician offered to refer the patient to the podiatrist for the callus and to book his eye screening.
The clinician scheduled a follow-up appointment in three months with a repeat HbA1c and kidney test.

findings.rationale: The note incorrectly states the dose of empagliflozin as 100 mg instead of the 10 mg mentioned in the transcript.

findings.note_span: Reduce gliclazide to 80 mg in the morning only.
findings.transcript_evidence: I'd like to reduce it to 80 milligrams in the morning only, and stop the teatime dose.
findings.rationale: The note omitted the critical instruction to stop the teatime dose of gliclazide, which is a key part of the agreed plan change.
